Hierarchical and cluster designs

Source: vignettes/hierarchical-designs.Rmd
hierarchical-designs.Rmd
library(cohortflow)

In many studies the rows of the data are not the only units that matter. Participants sit inside clusters (practices, schools, wards), clusters inside sites, and repeated measurements inside participants. Reporting needs counts at more than one level: the CONSORT extension for cluster trials (Campbell, Elbourne and Altman, BMJ 2004;328:702–8) asks for losses at each stage to be given for clusters and for participants.

cohortflow handles this by recording, at every step, how many distinct units were present at each level you declare.

Declaring the hierarchy

cf_hierarchy() names the levels, from finest to coarsest, and maps each to the column(s) that identify it:

cl <- mock_cluster_rct(n_clusters = 16, n_participants = 600, seed = 7)

h <- cf_hierarchy(
  participant = "participant_id",
  cluster = "cluster_id",
  site = "site_id"
)
h
#> Cohort hierarchy (finest → coarsest):
#>   ├─ participant  →  column: participant_id
#>   ├─ cluster  →  column: cluster_id
#>   └─ site  →  column: site_id

Pass it to apply_criteria() with hierarchy =. Nothing changes about which rows are kept; the flow just records the extra counts.

crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening", reason = "Failed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent") |>
  group_include(by = "cluster_id", ~ n() >= 20,
                label = "Cluster recruited 20 or more") |>
  randomise(by = "cluster_id", arms = "arm") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent")

flow <- apply_criteria(cl, crit, id = "participant_id", hierarchy = h)

Counts at every level

levels in as_attrition_tibble() returns one block per level (NULL means all of them):

as_attrition_tibble(flow, levels = c("participant", "cluster"))
#> # A tibble: 14 × 8
#>    row_type label indent_level     n n_removed n_consequential pct_removed level
#>    <chr>    <chr>        <int> <int>     <int>           <int>       <dbl> <chr>
#>  1 header   Asse…            0   600        NA              NA        NA   part…
#>  2 step     Pass…            1   600        68               0        11.3 part…
#>  3 step     Cons…            1   532        83               0        15.6 part…
#>  4 step     Clus…            1   449         0              37         0   part…
#>  5 step     Rand…            1   412         0               0         0   part…
#>  6 step     With…            1   412        18               0         4.4 part…
#>  7 final    Fina…            0   394        NA              NA        65.7 part…
#>  8 header   Asse…            0    15        NA              NA        NA   clus…
#>  9 step     Pass…            1    15         0               0         0   clus…
#> 10 step     Cons…            1    15         0               0         0   clus…
#> 11 step     Clus…            1    15         5               0        33.3 clus…
#> 12 step     Rand…            1    10         0               0         0   clus…
#> 13 step     With…            1    10         0               0         0   clus…

as_attrition_table() puts the levels side by side, which is the layout the CONSORT cluster extension describes. Each criterion reads across both levels at once:

as_attrition_table(
  flow,
  levels = c("participant", "cluster"),
  level_labels = c(participant = "Participants", cluster = "Clusters"),
  backend = "gt"
)

How units are counted

Two rules decide when a coarser unit counts as lost. They matter because a naive count of “distinct clusters among the excluded rows” gives the wrong answer.

Row-level steps count from the bottom up. A cluster is lost at a step only when its last remaining participant is removed there. Losing some of a cluster’s participants is not losing the cluster.

A small example makes this concrete. Cluster A has three participants and cluster B has two:

toy <- data.frame(
  pid = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2"),
  cluster = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B"),
  consented = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
)
toy_flow <- apply_criteria(
  toy,
  cf_criteria() |> include(~ consented, label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent"),
  id = "pid",
  hierarchy = cf_hierarchy(participant = "pid", cluster = "cluster")
)
as_attrition_tibble(toy_flow, levels = NULL)[, c("level", "label", "n", "n_removed")]
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   level       label                        n n_removed
#>   <chr>       <chr>                    <int>     <int>
#> 1 participant Assessed for eligibility     5        NA
#> 2 participant Consented                    5         3
#> 3 participant Final cohort                 2        NA
#> 4 cluster     Assessed for eligibility     2        NA
#> 5 cluster     Consented                    2         1
#> 6 cluster     Final cohort                 1        NA

Three participants were removed (one from A, two from B), but only one cluster, B, was lost, because A still has participants left.

Group-level steps count from the top down. group_include() and group_exclude() remove whole clusters, and their participants go with them. Those participants were not individually excluded, so they are reported in a separate n_consequential column rather than as n_removed. In the trial above, the cluster-size rule removed 5 clusters, and with them 37 participants who were otherwise eligible:

tbl <- as_attrition_tibble(flow, levels = c("participant", "cluster"))
tbl[tbl$label == "Cluster recruited 20 or more",
    c("level", "n", "n_removed", "n_consequential")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   level           n n_removed n_consequential
#>   <chr>       <int>     <int>           <int>
#> 1 participant   449         0              37
#> 2 cluster        15         5               0

This is the distinction the cluster extension draws between losing a cluster and losing participants.

Composite levels: stepped-wedge trials

A level can be identified by more than one column. In a stepped-wedge trial, each cluster contributes a cluster-period for every period of the roll-out, so the cluster-period is identified by cluster_id and period:

sw <- mock_stepped_wedge(n_clusters = 8, n_participants = 400,
                         n_periods = 4, n_sites = 2, seed = 3)

h_sw <- cf_hierarchy(
  observation = "event_id",
  cluster_period = c("cluster_id", "period"),
  cluster = "cluster_id"
)

crit_sw <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew") |>
  group_include(by = c("cluster_id", "period"), ~ n() >= 8,
                label = "Cluster-period has 8 or more")

flow_sw <- apply_criteria(sw, crit_sw, id = "event_id", hierarchy = h_sw)
as_attrition_table(
  flow_sw,
  levels = c("observation", "cluster_period", "cluster"),
  level_labels = c("Observations", "Cluster-periods", "Clusters"),
  backend = "gt"
)
Criterion
Observations
Cluster-periods
Clusters

The cluster-period rule removed 12 cluster-periods but only 3 whole clusters: the others still had at least one period with enough participants.

Stepped-wedge results are also often shown by site and period. group_x and group_y repeat the attrition table for each combination; see Attrition tables.

Characteristics at the cluster level

as_characteristics_table() and stack_cohorts() take a level argument to describe units at that level rather than rows. Every variable must be constant within a unit, as cluster-level variables such as site and arm are:

as_characteristics_tibble(
  flow,
  vars = c("site_id", "arm"),
  steps = list(0, "Cluster recruited 20 or more"),
  level = "cluster",
  wide = TRUE
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   variable level        Assessed for eligibility (n = 1…¹ Cluster recruited 20…²
#>   <chr>    <chr>        <chr>                             <chr>                 
#> 1 site_id  S1           1 (6.7%)                          1 (10.0%)             
#> 2 site_id  S2           7 (46.7%)                         4 (40.0%)             
#> 3 site_id  S3           7 (46.7%)                         5 (50.0%)             
#> 4 arm      Control      8 (53.3%)                         5 (50.0%)             
#> 5 arm      Intervention 7 (46.7%)                         5 (50.0%)             
#> # ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​`Assessed for eligibility (n = 15)`,
#> #   ²​`Cluster recruited 20 or more (n = 10)`

Limits

  • levels cannot be combined with group_x, group_y, branch_by or count_by in the same table.
  • as_consort_diagram() draws one level at a time: rows by default, or a hierarchy level with count_by (count_by = "cluster" draws a cluster-flow diagram). For a cluster trial, draw the participant-level diagram and report cluster counts in the attrition table alongside it.
  • cf_hierarchy() does not require strict nesting, but its counts are easiest to read when each level nests in the next.
